title: Proof
body_md:
This map is pretty natural. Indeed, let's construct an inverse. Suppose that there are $k$ circles in $\underline{\lambda}\overline{\mu}$ denoted $C_1, \ldots, C_k$. Then observe that any monomial in $\mathcal{M}(\underline{\lambda}\overline{\mu})$ is of the form $\prod_{i=1}^{k} X_{t(C_i)}^{p_i}$, where $p_i \in \{ 0,1 \}$ for $1 \leq i \leq k$. Then we set
    $$(\varphi_{\underline{\lambda}\overline{\mu}})^{-1}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k} X_{t(C_i)}^{p_i}\right) = \underline{\lambda}\nu\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k} X_{t(C_i)}^{p_i}\right)\overline{\mu}$$
    where $\nu\left(\prod_{i=1}^{k} X_{t(C_i)}^{p_i}\right)$ orients the circle $C_i$ clockwisely if $p_i = 1$ and counterclockwisely if $p_i = 0$, and has no choice for the open arcs. Finally we extend this map linearly.

\label{def:4.24}
    We will denote $\mathbb{D} _n^0$ by $\mathbb{D} _n$, and from now on we will work exclusively with $\mathbb{D} _n$. This choice is motivated by the fact that $\mathbb{D} _n^0$ is the algebra most studied in the literature. It is shown in~\cite{EhrigStroppel2016a} that the category of finite dimensional $\mathbb{D} _n$-modules is equivalent to the category of perverse sheaves on the isotropic Grassmannians of type $D_n$ or $B_{n-1}$. We note however that $\mathbb{D} _n^1$ is also interesting, and all the results cited in the next sections remain valid for $\mathbb{D} _n^1$ as well.

title: Proof
body_md:
If $\lambda \neq \mu$, suppose by contradiction that
    $$\text{dim}_\Bbbk \left( e_\lambda ( \Bbbk Q_n/I_n )_2 e_\mu \right) > 1$$
    Then there exist two paths $p$ and $q$ of length $2$ from $e_\lambda$ to $e_\mu$ such that $[p]$ and $[q]$ are linearly independant in $\Bbbk Q_n/I_n$. This means that $p-q \not \in I_n$, but $p$ and $q$ define a square, so we should have $p-q \in I_n$ thanks to Theorem~\ref{thm:5.15}. This contradiction tells us that
    $$\text{dim}_\Bbbk \left( e_\lambda ( \Bbbk Q_n/I_n )_2 e_\mu \right) \leq 1$$
    Now if $\lambda = \mu$, the relations at vertex $e_\lambda$ in $I_n$ tell us that $e_\lambda( \Bbbk Q_n/I_n )_2 e_\lambda$ is spanned by the $2$-cycles of the form $x_\lambda^{\mu_i} y_\lambda^{\mu_i}$ for $1 \leq i \leq \text{def}(\lambda)$. So we have that
    $$\text{dim}_\Bbbk \left( e_\lambda ( \Bbbk Q_n/I_n )_2 e_\lambda \right) \leq \text{def}(\lambda)$$
    as wanted.

title: Proof

As we said before, we just need to verify that $\overline{\omega}$ is a bijection in degree $2$. And since $\overline{\omega}$ is surjective, we just need to verify that
    $$\text{dim}_\Bbbk \left( e_\lambda ( \Bbbk Q_n/I_n )_2 e_\mu \right) = \text{dim}_\Bbbk \left( e_\lambda ( \mathbb{D} _n )_2 e_\mu \right)$$

An $A_\infty$-algebra over $\Bbbk$ is a graded vector space $A = \bigoplus_{k \in \mathbb{Z} } A^k$ endowed with graded maps
    $$m_n : A^{\otimes n} \to A, \ n \geq 1$$
    of degree $2-n$, satisfying the following relations
    $$m_1m_1 = 0, \qquad m_1m_2 = m_2(m_1 \otimes \textbf{1} + \textbf{1} \otimes m_1)$$
    $$m_2(\textbf{1} \otimes m_2 - m_2 \otimes \textbf{1}) = m_1m_3 + m_3(m_1 \otimes \textbf{1} \otimes \textbf{1} + \textbf{1} \otimes m_1 \otimes \textbf{1} + \textbf{1} \otimes \textbf{1} \otimes m_1)$$
    and more generally, for $n \geq 1$
    $$\sum_{r+s+t=n} (-1)^{r+st}m_{r+t+1}(\textbf{1}^{\otimes r} \otimes m_s \otimes \textbf{1}^{\otimes t}) = 0$$
    where $\textbf{1}$ denotes the identity map of $A$.

label: defmethod
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{defmethod}
A first-order deformation of a reduction system \(R = \{(s,\varphi_s)\}_{s\in S}\) is a reduction system
\[
\widetilde{R} = \{(s,\varphi_s + \widetilde{\varphi}_s\, t)\}_{s\in S}
\]
over \(\Bbbk Q \otimes_\Bbbk \Bbbk [t]/(t^2)\), where \(\widetilde{\varphi}_s \in \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S\), such that \(\widetilde{R}\) is reduction-unique. \\
Equivalently, \(\widetilde{\varphi}\) defines a morphism
\[
\widetilde{\varphi} \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\Bbbk Q_0^e}(\Bbbk S, \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S), 
\quad s \mapsto \widetilde{\varphi}_s.
\]
We say that \(\widetilde{\varphi}\) defines a first-order deformation of \(R\) if it is a \(2\)-cocycle in the cochain complex associated to the Bardzell--Chouhy--Solotar resolution from~\cite{ChouhrSolotar2015}. In other words this means that $\tilde{\varphi}$ is a \(2\)-cocycle if and only if for any overlap ambiguity $pqr$ of length $3$, we have 
$$(p \star q) \star r  = p \star (q \star r) \text{ mod } t^2$$
where
$$u \star v = \left\{
    \begin{array}{cc}
        uv & \mbox{if } uv \not \in S \\
        \varphi_{uv} + t\tilde{\varphi}_{uv} & \mbox{if } uv \in S
    \end{array} \right.$$
Two first-order deformations $\widetilde{R} = \{(s,\varphi_s + \widetilde{\varphi}_s t)\}_{s\in S}$ and $\widetilde{R}' = \{(s,\varphi_s + \widetilde{\varphi}'_s t)\}_{s\in S}$ are equivalent if there exists
\[
\psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\Bbbk Q_0^e}(\Bbbk Q_1, \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S)
\]
such that for all \(s \in S\),
\[
\widetilde{\varphi}_s - \widetilde{\varphi}'_s = \delta(\psi)(s).
\]
Here
\[
\delta : \mathrm{Hom}_{\Bbbk Q_0^e}(\Bbbk Q_1, \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S)
\longrightarrow
\mathrm{Hom}_{\Bbbk Q_0^e}(\Bbbk S, \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S)
\]
is given by
\[
\delta(\psi)(s) = T(\psi)(s - \varphi_s),
\]
where \(T(\psi) : \Bbbk Q \to \Bbbk \mathrm{Irr}_S\) is defined on a path \(p = a_1 \cdots a_m\) by
\[
T(\psi)(p)
=
\sum_{i=1}^m
\sigma\pi(a_1 \cdots a_{i-1}\,\psi(a_i)\,a_{i+1} \cdots a_m).
\]
Here \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) are arrows in \(Q\), \(\pi : \Bbbk Q \to \Bbbk Q/I\) is the natural projection, and \(\sigma : \Bbbk Q/I \to \Bbbk\mathrm{Irr}_S\) is the inverse of \(\pi|_{\mathrm{Irr}_S}\). In other words, \(\sigma\pi(p)\) is obtained by reducing \(p\) with respect to \(R\) until it becomes irreducible.

with some conditions on the $\alpha_i$'s that we are going to compute. We recall from Definition~\ref{defmethod}, that $\tilde{\varphi}$ is a \(2\)-cocycle if and only if for any overlap ambiguity $pqr$ of length $3$, we have 
$$(p \star q) \star r  = p \star (q \star r) \text{ mod } t^2$$
where
$$u \star v = \left\{
    \begin{array}{cc}
        uv & \mbox{if } uv \not \in S \\
        \varphi_{uv} + t\tilde{\varphi}_{uv} & \mbox{if } uv \in S
    \end{array} \right.$$
For example, note that the overlap ambiguity $\overline{y}_{10}\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1$ admits a unique parallel irreducible path of length $5$ given by $\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2$, that we will denote $p$. Thus we can compute
\begin{align*}
    \overline{y}_{10} \star (\overline{y}_1 \star \overline{x}_1) &= \overline{y}_{10} \star (-\overline{x}_2\overline{y}_2 + t(\alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2 + \alpha_2\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_4\overline{y}_4\overline{y}_2)) &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= -(\overline{y}_{10} \star \overline{x}_2) \star \overline{y}_2 + t(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)p &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= -(-\overline{y}_{9}\overline{y}_{8} + t\alpha_{12}\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3 ) \star \overline{y}_2 + t(\alpha_1 - \alpha_2)p &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= \overline{y}_{9} \star (\overline{y}_8 \star \overline{y}_2) + t(- \alpha_{12} + \alpha_1 - \alpha_2)p  &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= \overline{y}_{9} \star (-\overline{x}_{9}\overline{y}_{10} + t\alpha_{23}\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2 ) + t(- \alpha_{12} + \alpha_1 - \alpha_2)p  &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= t(\alpha_{23} - \alpha_{12} + \alpha_1 - \alpha_2)p  &\text{ mod } t^2 \\
    &= (\overline{y}_{10} \star \overline{y}_1) \star \overline{x}_1 = 0 &\text{ mod } t^2
\end{align*}
So we deduce that
$$\alpha_1 - \alpha_2 - \alpha_{12} + \alpha_{23} = 0$$
The other conditions can be computed similarly and we find
\begin{align*}
& \alpha_1 - \alpha_2 - \alpha_{12} + \alpha_{23} = 0 \\
& \alpha_1 - \alpha_2 - \alpha_{11} + \alpha_{24} = 0 \\
& \alpha_8 - \alpha_9 + \alpha_{13} + \alpha_{15} + \alpha_{19} + \alpha_{20} = 0 \\
& \alpha_8 - \alpha_9 + \alpha_{14} + \alpha_{16} + \alpha_{21} + \alpha_{22} = 0 \\
& \alpha_7 - \alpha_{10} + \alpha_{14} + \alpha_{17} + \alpha_{20} = 0 \\
& \alpha_7 - \alpha_{10} + \alpha_{13} + \alpha_{18} + \alpha_{22} = 0 \\
& \alpha_3 - 2\alpha_5 - \alpha_{12} - \alpha_{15} + \alpha_{17} + \alpha_{19} - \alpha_{23} = 0 \\
& \alpha_3 - 2\alpha_4 - \alpha_{11} - \alpha_{16} + \alpha_{18} + \alpha_{21} - \alpha_{24} = 0
\end{align*}
You can observe that these eight equations are linearly independant because a new variable is introduced in each equation. Thus the dimension of the cocycle space is $24-8 = 16$. \\
Now we need to compute the dimension of the subspace of the coboundaries. We recall that a coboundary is an element $\psi \in \text{Hom}_{\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_0^e}(\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_1, \Bbbk \text{Irr}_{\overline{S}_4})_2$, so in other words $\psi$ is a degree $2$ map that fixes the endpoints, and thus $\psi$ has the following form
    $$\psi_{\overline{y}_1}
= \beta_1\overline{x}_2\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1,
\quad
\psi_{\overline{x}_1}
= \beta_2\overline{x}_1\overline{x}_2\overline{y}_2,$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_2}

\quad
\psi_{\overline{x}_2}

+ \beta_7\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_4\overline{y}_4

\qquad
\psi_{\overline{x}_5}

$$\psi_{\overline{y}_6} = \beta_{19}\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_6,
\qquad\quad
\psi_{\overline{x}_6} = \beta_{20}\overline{x}_6\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_7,$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_7}
= \beta_{21}\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7,
\qquad
\psi_{\overline{x}_7}
= \beta_{22}\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9,$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_8}

\qquad
\psi_{\overline{x}_8}
= \beta_{25}\overline{x}_8\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9 + \beta_{26}\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7,$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_9}
= 0,
\qquad
\psi_{\overline{x}_9}
= 0,\qquad\psi_{\overline{y}_{10}}
= 0,
\qquad
\psi_{\overline{x}_{10}}
= 0,$$
    where $\beta_1, \ldots, \beta_{26} \in \Bbbk$. If $\delta(\psi)_s = \tilde{\varphi}_s$ for every $s \in \overline{S}_4$, then using Definition~\ref{defmethod} to compute $\delta(\psi)_s$, we obtain

Let $\{ (s, \varphi_s + \tilde{\varphi}_s t) \}_{s \in \overline{S}_4}$ be a first order deformation of $\overline{R}_4$ corresponding to a cocycle in $\text{HH}^2_4(\mathbb{D} _4,\mathbb{D} _4)$. Then $\tilde{\varphi} \in \text{Hom}_{\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_0^e}(\Bbbk \overline{S}_4, \Bbbk \text{Irr}_{\overline{S}_4})_4$, so in other words $\tilde{\varphi}$ is a degree $4$ map that fixes the endpoints, and thus $\tilde{\varphi}_s$ has the following form for $s \in \overline{S}_4$
    $$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1}
= \alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2
+ \alpha_2\overline{x}_{10}\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2
+ \alpha_3\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_{10},
$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_2\overline{x}_2}
= \alpha_4\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3
+ \alpha_5\overline{x}_8\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3
+ \alpha_6\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_8,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_3\overline{x}_3}
= \alpha_7\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5,
\quad
\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_4\overline{x}_4}
= \alpha_8\overline{x}_6\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_6,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_3\overline{x}_4}
= \alpha_{9}\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_6,
\quad
\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_4\overline{x}_3}
= \alpha_{10}\overline{x}_6\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_{10}\overline{y}_1}
= \alpha_{11}\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1,
\quad
\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{x}_1\overline{x}_{10}}
= \alpha_{12}\overline{x}_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_6\overline{y}_4}
= \alpha_{13}\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3,
\quad \tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{x}_4\overline{x}_6}
= \alpha_{14}\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7,
$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_8\overline{y}_2}
= \alpha_{15}\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2,
\quad
\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_8}
= \alpha_{16}\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_s = 0 \quad \text{else},$$
for $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_{16} \in \Bbbk$ without any condition on them because none of the overlaps admit a parallel irreducible path of length $7$. \\
Now we need to compute the dimension of the subspace of the coboundaries. We recall that a coboundary is an element $\psi \in \text{Hom}_{\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_0^e}(\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_1, \Bbbk \text{Irr}_{\overline{S}_4})_4$, so in other words $\psi$ is a degree $4$ map that fixes the endpoints, and thus $\psi$ has the following form
    $$\psi_{\overline{y}_1}
= \beta_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1 + \beta_2\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_4\overline{y}_4\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1 ,
\quad
\psi_{\overline{x}_1}
= \beta_3\overline{x}_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2 + \beta_4\overline{x}_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_4\overline{y}_4\overline{y}_2,$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_2}
= \beta_5\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2
+ \beta_6\overline{x}_8\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2
+ \beta_7\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_{7}\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_{10},$$
$$\psi_{\overline{x}_2}
= \beta_8\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3
+ \beta_9\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_8

body_md:
Let $\{ (s, \varphi_s + \tilde{\varphi}_s t) \}_{s \in \overline{S}_4}$ be a first order deformation of $\overline{R}_4$ corresponding to a cocycle in $\text{HH}^2_6(\mathbb{D} _4,\mathbb{D} _4)$. Then $\tilde{\varphi} \in \text{Hom}_{\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_0^e}(\Bbbk \overline{S}_4, \Bbbk \text{Irr}_{\overline{S}_4})_6$, so in other words $\tilde{\varphi}$ is a degree $6$ map that fixes the endpoints, and thus $\tilde{\varphi}_s$ has the following form for $s \in \overline{S}_4$
    $$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1}
= \alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2,
$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_2\overline{x}_2}
= \alpha_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3,$$
$$\tilde{\varphi}_s = 0 \quad \text{else},$$
for $\alpha_1, \alpha_{2} \in \Bbbk$ without any condition on them because none of the overlaps admit a parallel irreducible path of length $9$. \\
Consider now the coboundary $\psi \in \text{Hom}_{\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_0^e}(\Bbbk (\overline{Q}_4)_1, \Bbbk \text{Irr}_{\overline{S}_4})_6$ defined by
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_1}
= -\alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1,
$$
$$\psi_{\overline{y}_3}
= \alpha_2\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{x}_9\overline{y}_9\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3,$$
$$\psi_{y_i} = \psi_{x_i} = 0 \quad \text{else},$$
Then if we compute
\begin{align*}
\delta(\psi)_{\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1}
&= T(\psi)(\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1 + \overline{x}_2\overline{y}_2) \\
&= \sigma\pi(\psi_{\overline{y}_1}\overline{x}_1 + \overline{y}_1\psi_{\overline{x}_1} + \psi_{\overline{x}_2}\overline{y}_2 + \overline{x}_2\psi_{\overline{y}_2} ) \\
&= \sigma\pi(-\alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1) \\
&= \alpha_1\overline{x}_2\overline{x}_3\overline{x}_5\overline{x}_7\overline{y}_7\overline{y}_5\overline{y}_3\overline{y}_2 = \tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_1\overline{x}_1}
\end{align*}
and similarly
$$\delta(\psi)_{\overline{y}_2\overline{x}_2} = \tilde{\varphi}_{\overline{y}_2\overline{x}_2}$$
Thus we have that $\delta(\psi) = \tilde{\varphi}$ and hence $\tilde{\varphi}$ is trivial. So we deduce that
$$\text{HH}^2_6(\mathbb{D} _4, \mathbb{D} _4) = 0$$
as wanted.
